subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Reference frames and what makes one inertial
Galilean relativity: the same mechanics in every inertial frame
The Lorentz transformation and the Lorentz factor
The space–time interval is the same for every observer
The slope of a world line gives the speed
Muon decay as evidence for time dilation and length contraction

questions.q: A passenger on a train moving at constant velocity says that the platform is moving backwards at 20 m s⁻¹. A person standing on the platform says that the train is moving forwards at 20 m s⁻¹. Which statement is correct?
options: Only the platform observer is correct, because the ground is the frame truly at rest.
Both are correct: each describes the motion relative to their own inertial frame.
Only the platform observer is correct, as a moving frame cannot be inertial.
Only one can be correct, as velocity belongs to the object, not to the observer.
optionWhy: A student who believes the ground is the one frame that is really at rest picks this. The ground itself moves relative to the Sun; no inertial frame is preferred.
Motion is always described relative to a reference frame. The train and the platform are both inertial frames, and neither is preferred, so both descriptions are equally valid.
A student who thinks an inertial frame must be at rest picks this. A frame moving at constant velocity is inertial, so the passenger's frame is as valid as the platform's.

A student who thinks each object has a single true velocity picks this. Velocity is always measured relative to a frame, so the platform has one velocity in the train's frame and the train another in the platform's frame, and both are valid.
questions.explain: Motion is always described relative to a reference frame. The train and the platform are both inertial frames, and neither is preferred, so both descriptions are equally valid.
questions.working: Train frame: platform velocity −20 m s⁻¹. Platform frame: train velocity +20 m s⁻¹. Both frames are inertial (constant velocity), so both descriptions are valid.

questions.q: Observers in two inertial frames, S and S′, which move at a constant velocity relative to each other, both study a puck that is being pushed across ice and is accelerating. Which quantity do they measure to have the same value?
options: The acceleration of the puck at any instant
The velocity of the puck at any given instant
The linear momentum of the puck at any instant
The position of the puck at any instant
optionWhy: u′ = u − v with v constant, so Δu′ = Δu and the accelerations are equal. Both observers therefore find the same resultant force, F = ma: Newton's laws are the same in both frames.
A student who thinks an object has one velocity for all observers picks this. The velocities differ by the relative velocity of the frames, u′ = u − v.
A student who confuses 'conserved' with 'the same in every frame' picks this. Momentum mu depends on the velocity, which differs between the frames.
A student who thinks positions are the same in every frame picks this. Positions are measured from each frame's own origin, and the origins move apart: x′ = x − vt.
questions.explain: u′ = u − v with v constant, so Δu′ = Δu and the accelerations are equal. Both observers therefore find the same resultant force, F = ma: Newton's laws are the same in both frames.
questions.working: Galilean: u′ = u − v, v constant → a′ = Δu′/Δt = Δu/Δt = a. Velocity, momentum and position differ between the frames.

questions.q: A ball rolls along a platform at 5.0 m s⁻¹. Frame S is the platform; frame S′ is a train moving at 25 m s⁻¹ in the positive x-direction relative to the platform. The origins of S and S′ coincide at t = 0. At t = 12 s the ball is at x = 450 m in S. What is the ball's position x′ in S′ at that instant?
optionWhy: A student who adds vt, thinking positions in a forward-moving frame are larger, calculates 450 + 300 = 750 m. The origin of S′ has moved 300 m towards the ball, so vt is subtracted.
A student who uses the ball's speed in the transformation calculates 450 − 5.0 × 12 = 390 m. The v in x′ = x − vt is the velocity of frame S′ relative to S, 25 m s⁻¹.
A student who thinks an event has the same position in every frame gives 450 m. The origin of S′ is 300 m from the origin of S at t = 12 s, so the positions differ.
x′ = x − vt, where v is the velocity of S′ relative to S: x′ = 450 m − (25 m s⁻¹)(12 s) = 450 m − 300 m = 150 m.
questions.explain: x′ = x − vt, where v is the velocity of S′ relative to S: x′ = 450 m − (25 m s⁻¹)(12 s) = 450 m − 300 m = 150 m.
questions.working: x′ = x − vt = 450 m − (25 m s⁻¹ × 12 s) = 450 m − 300 m = 150 m. (The ball's own speed of 5.0 m s⁻¹ is not needed.)

questions.q: A spacecraft moves directly away from a laser at 0.50c relative to the laser. Applying u′ = u − v, an observer on the spacecraft should measure the laser light passing at 0.50c. Experiments of this kind find c for every inertial observer. What should be concluded?
options: The experiments must contain an error, since u′ = u − v is common sense.
Light is an exception as it is massless; u′ = u − v holds for massive bodies.
u′ = u − v is only an approximation, valid when speeds are much less than c.
The ship only appears to measure c; relative to it the light really passes at 0.50c.
optionWhy: A student who treats Galilean addition as exact common sense at all speeds blames the measurement. Many independent experiments, with different methods, all find c for every inertial observer; the equation, not the measurement, is at fault.

A student who thinks light is an exception because it is massless picks this. The Galilean rule also fails for fast electrons and muons; the flaw is the assumption t′ = t, which applies to everything.

The Galilean result follows from the assumption t′ = t. It matches experiment at everyday speeds but fails for light and for any object moving at a speed comparable to c. It is replaced by the relativistic u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²).

A student who thinks the laser's frame gives the "true" speed, so the ship's measurement is only apparent, picks this. The ship's frame is as valid as any other, and the ship's observer really does measure c; the Galilean prediction of 0.50c is simply wrong.
questions.explain: The Galilean result follows from the assumption t′ = t. It matches experiment at everyday speeds but fails for light and for any object moving at a speed comparable to c. It is replaced by the relativistic u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²).
questions.working: Galilean prediction in spacecraft frame: u′ = c − 0.50c = 0.50c. Measured: c. The Galilean equation is therefore only an approximation; special relativity replaces it.

questions.q: Frame S′ moves at v = 0.80c in the positive x-direction relative to frame S, and the origins coincide at t = t′ = 0. An event occurs at x = 900 m, t = 1.0 μs in S. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the time t′ of the event in S′?
optionWhy: γ = 1.67. vx/c² = (0.80 × 3.00 × 10⁸ × 900)/(3.00 × 10⁸)² = 2.4 × 10⁻⁶ s. t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) = 1.67 × (1.0 − 2.4) μs = 1.67 × (−1.4 μs) = −2.3 μs. The event happens before the origins pass, according to S′.
A student who assumes time is the same in every frame (t′ = t) gives 1.0 μs. In special relativity t′ depends on the position of the event through the vx/c² term.
A student who leaves out γ calculates t − vx/c² = −1.4 μs. The bracket must be multiplied by γ = 1.67.
A student who applies time dilation to the event's time coordinate calculates γt = 1.67 × 1.0 = 1.7 μs. The full transformation t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) includes the position-dependent term.
questions.explain: γ = 1.67. vx/c² = (0.80 × 3.00 × 10⁸ × 900)/(3.00 × 10⁸)² = 2.4 × 10⁻⁶ s. t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) = 1.67 × (1.0 − 2.4) μs = 1.67 × (−1.4 μs) = −2.3 μs. The event happens before the origins pass, according to S′.

questions.q: An aircraft flies at 250 m s⁻¹ relative to the ground and a faster jet flies in the same direction at 800 m s⁻¹. A student compares u′ = u − v = 550 m s⁻¹ for the jet in the aircraft's frame with the relativistic value from u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²). Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. Which evaluation is correct?
options: The relativistic equation cannot be used, as relativity applies only to speeds near c.
u − v is exact at these speeds, so the relativistic equation gives a slightly wrong value.
uv/c² ≈ 2 × 10⁻¹², so the Galilean value differs from the relativistic one by a negligible amount.
uv/c² ≈ 7 × 10⁻⁴, so the Galilean value is in error by about 0.07 %, which is a clearly measurable amount.
optionWhy: A student who thinks relativity switches on only near c picks this. The relativistic equation is valid at every speed; at 800 m s⁻¹ it simply gives a result extremely close to the Galilean one.
A student who treats Galilean addition as exact picks this. The relativistic equation is the exact one; the Galilean result is the approximation, though the difference is negligible here.
uv/c² = (800 × 250)/(3.00 × 10⁸)² = 2.2 × 10⁻¹². The relativistic value differs from 550 m s⁻¹ by about 1 × 10⁻⁹ m s⁻¹, so u′ = u − v is an excellent approximation at everyday speeds.
A student who divides by c instead of c² gets 800 × 250/(3.00 × 10⁸) = 6.7 × 10⁻⁴. That quantity has a unit (m s⁻¹) and cannot be subtracted from 1; with c² the term is 2.2 × 10⁻¹².
questions.explain: uv/c² = (800 × 250)/(3.00 × 10⁸)² = 2.2 × 10⁻¹². The relativistic value differs from 550 m s⁻¹ by about 1 × 10⁻⁹ m s⁻¹, so u′ = u − v is an excellent approximation at everyday speeds.

questions.q: In frame S, two events occur at the same place, 5.0 μs apart. In frame S′, which moves relative to S, the two events are 1200 m apart. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the time interval between the events in S′?
options: 3.0 μs
9.0 μs
5.0 μs
6.4 μs
optionWhy: A student who takes (Δs)² = (cΔt)² + (Δx)² writes 1500² = (cΔt′)² + 1200² and gets cΔt′ = 900 m, Δt′ = 3.0 μs. With the correct minus sign, (cΔt′)² = 1500² + 1200².
A student who uses Δs = cΔt − Δx without squares writes 1500 = cΔt′ − 1200, giving cΔt′ = 2700 m and 9.0 μs. Only the squared combination is invariant.
A student who assumes time intervals are the same in every frame gives 5.0 μs. Δt changes between frames; it is (Δs)² that is invariant.

questions.q: An astronaut measures the length of her spacecraft. An observer on Earth, relative to whom the spacecraft moves at 0.60c along its length, also measures it. Which statement is correct?
options: The astronaut measures the proper length, the shortest length found by any inertial observer.
The Earth observer measures the proper length, as the Earth is the frame that is truly at rest.
The astronaut measures the proper length, the longest length found by any inertial observer.
Both measure the same length; the Earth observer merely sees it shorter because light takes time.
optionWhy: A student who reasons that proper length must be the shortest, like proper time, picks this. Proper time is the shortest interval but proper length is the longest length: L = L₀/γ ≤ L₀.
A student who treats the Earth as truly at rest picks this. The proper length is measured in the frame in which the object is at rest, which here is the astronaut's frame.
The proper length is measured in the object's rest frame, the astronaut's. Every observer moving along its length measures L = L₀/γ, which is shorter.
A student who thinks length contraction is an optical effect picks this. After allowing for light travel time the Earth observer still measures L = L₀/γ, a real difference.
questions.explain: The proper length is measured in the object's rest frame, the astronaut's. Every observer moving along its length measures L = L₀/γ, which is shorter.
questions.working: Proper length L₀: measured in the rest frame of the object (astronaut). Earth: L = L₀/γ = L₀/1.25 = 0.80L₀.

questions.q: Spacecraft A and B pass each other at a relative speed of 0.60c. Each carries an identical clock. The astronaut in A says that B's clock runs slow, and the astronaut in B says that A's clock runs slow. Which evaluation is correct?
options: Only one can be correct: the clock that is really moving is the one that runs slow.
Neither is correct: the clocks only appear slow because light from them takes time to arrive.
Both are correct: each measures the clock moving relative to them to run slow, by γ = 1.25.
Neither is correct: the two effects cancel, so each measures the other's clock at the normal rate.
optionWhy: A student who believes one spacecraft is 'really' moving picks this. There is no absolute rest; each astronaut can regard their own craft as at rest, and both measurements are valid.
A student who treats time dilation as a signal-delay illusion picks this. Each observer's result remains after correcting for light travel time; it is a real measured effect.

By the first postulate neither inertial frame is preferred, so time dilation is reciprocal. Each observer measures the other's clock to run slow by γ = 1/√(1 − 0.60²) = 1.25. The relativity of simultaneity makes the two results consistent.
A student who sees reciprocal time dilation as a contradiction picks this. The two measurements compare different pairs of events in different frames, so they do not cancel; each is valid.
questions.explain: By the first postulate neither inertial frame is preferred, so time dilation is reciprocal. Each observer measures the other's clock to run slow by γ = 1/√(1 − 0.60²) = 1.25. The relativity of simultaneity makes the two results consistent.
questions.working: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.60²) = 1/0.80 = 1.25. Each frame measures the other's clock interval as Δt = 1.25Δt₀.

questions.q: A cube has edges of proper length 2.0 m. It moves at 0.80c relative to an observer, parallel to one of its edges. Which statement gives the dimensions of the cube as measured by this observer?
options: Its edge along the motion is 3.3 m; its other two edges are still 2.0 m each.
Its edge along the motion is 1.2 m; its other two edges are 2.0 m each.
All three of its edges are 1.2 m, because every dimension contracts by γ.
All three of its edges are 2.0 m, because a moving object merely looks shorter.
optionWhy: A student who multiplies by γ, as in time dilation, gets 2.0 × 1.67 = 3.3 m. Lengths are divided by γ: the moving edge is measured as L = L₀/γ = 1.2 m, shorter than its proper length.

γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1.67, so the edge parallel to the motion is measured as L = L₀/γ = 2.0/1.67 = 1.2 m. Length contraction acts only along the direction of relative motion; the two perpendicular edges keep their proper length of 2.0 m.

A student who applies the contraction to every dimension picks this. Only the length parallel to the relative velocity is contracted; lengths perpendicular to the motion are the same in every inertial frame, so the other two edges are measured as 2.0 m.

A student who treats length contraction as an appearance caused by light travel time picks this. The contracted length is what the observer measures with rulers at rest in their own frame, after any signal delay is allowed for: the edge along the motion is genuinely measured as 1.2 m.
questions.explain: γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1.67, so the edge parallel to the motion is measured as L = L₀/γ = 2.0/1.67 = 1.2 m. Length contraction acts only along the direction of relative motion; the two perpendicular edges keep their proper length of 2.0 m.
questions.working:
γ = 1/√(1 − 0.80²) = 1/√0.36 = 1/0.60 = 1.67.
Only the edge parallel to the relative velocity is contracted: L = L₀/γ = 2.0 m × 0.60 = 1.2 m.
The two edges perpendicular to the motion are unchanged at 2.0 m. The observer measures a block 1.2 m × 2.0 m × 2.0 m.

questions.q: Two events are simultaneous in frame S and are 1200 m apart along the x-axis. Frame S′ moves at 0.60c along the x-axis relative to S. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of the time interval between the events in S′?
options: 2.4 μs
3.0 μs
1.9 μs
4.0 μs
optionWhy: A student who leaves out γ gives vΔx/c² = 2.4 μs. The Lorentz transformation multiplies the bracket by γ = 1.25.
A student who divides by γ gets 2.4/1.25 = 1.9 μs. In t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) the bracket is multiplied by γ.

A student who thinks the time difference is the light travel time between the events calculates Δx/c = 1200/(3.00 × 10⁸) = 4.0 μs. The relativity of simultaneity comes from the vx/c² term, not from signal delay.

questions.q: A space–time diagram for frame S (axes x and ct) also shows the axes x′ and ct′ of a frame S′ moving relative to S. How are the scales on the ct′ and x′ axes determined?
options: They are set by lines of constant space–time interval, so their units differ from those on ct and x.
They are identical to the scales on ct and x, because all four axes are measured in metres.
They are shrunk by γ, because moving clocks run slow and moving lengths are contracted.
They are stretched by γ on ct′ and shrunk by γ on x′, by time dilation and length contraction.
optionWhy: The guide states that the scales are not the same and are defined by lines of constant space–time interval. The curve (ct)² − x² = 1 unit² crosses ct′ at ct′ = 1; on S's diagram that point lies further from the origin than ct = 1.
A student who assumes axes with the same unit share one scale picks this. Same unit does not mean same drawn scale; the scales are fixed by lines of constant interval.

A student who builds the headline results into the drawing picks this. As drawn on S's diagram, a unit on a primed axis is longer, and it is found from a line of constant interval, not by dividing by γ.

A student who maps 'time dilation' onto a stretched time axis and 'length contraction' onto a shrunk space axis picks this. Both primed units are set by the invariant hyperbolae, and on S's diagram both appear longer than the unprimed units by the same factor, √((1 + v²/c²)/(1 − v²/c²)); neither axis is shrunk.
questions.explain: The guide states that the scales are not the same and are defined by lines of constant space–time interval. The curve (ct)² − x² = 1 unit² crosses ct′ at ct′ = 1; on S's diagram that point lies further from the origin than ct = 1.
questions.working: Scale on ct′: where (ct)² − x² = 1 crosses the ct′ axis (x = βct), ct = γ and x = βγ, so the distance from the origin on S's diagram is γ√(1 + β²) = √((1 + β²)/(1 − β²)) > 1. By symmetry, x² − (ct)² = 1 crosses the x′ axis at the same distance. Both primed units are longer than the unprimed units by the same factor.

questions.q: A space–time diagram for frame S has axes x and ct in light-years (ly). Frame S′ moves at 0.50c along +x; its ct′ axis and x′ axis are each tilted by the same angle towards the 45° line, the x′ axis rising 0.50 ly of ct for each 1 ly of x. Event P is at (x = 0, ct = 2.0 ly) and event Q at (x = 4.0 ly, ct = 2.0 ly). What is the order of P and Q in S′?
options: P and Q are simultaneous, because they lie on one line parallel to the x axis of S.
P occurs before Q, because Q lies further along the x′ axis, which tilts upwards.
P occurs before Q, because light from Q takes longer to reach an observer standing at x = 0.
Q occurs before P, as Q lies below the line through P parallel to the x′ axis.
optionWhy: A student who assumes simultaneity is the same in every frame picks this. A line parallel to the x axis joins events simultaneous in S only; simultaneity in S′ is read along lines parallel to the x′ axis.
A student who reads the tilt the wrong way picks this. The upward tilt means the S′ simultaneity line through P passes above Q, so Q happens first in S′, consistent with t′ = γ(t − vx/c²).
A student who dates events by when light arrives picks this. The order of events in a frame is set by its time coordinates, not by signal arrival; in S′, Q has the earlier time coordinate.

Lines parallel to the x′ axis join events simultaneous in S′. The line through P rises 0.50 ly per ly, so at x = 4.0 ly it is at ct = 4.0 ly. Q, at ct = 2.0 ly, lies below it, so Q is earlier in S′. Check: cΔt′ = γ(cΔt − (v/c)Δx) = 1.15 × (0 − 2.0 ly) < 0.
questions.explain: Lines parallel to the x′ axis join events simultaneous in S′. The line through P rises 0.50 ly per ly, so at x = 4.0 ly it is at ct = 4.0 ly. Q, at ct = 2.0 ly, lies below it, so Q is earlier in S′. Check: cΔt′ = γ(cΔt − (v/c)Δx) = 1.15 × (0 − 2.0 ly) < 0.
questions.working: x′-axis slope: Δ(ct)/Δx = v/c = 0.50. Line through P parallel to x′: ct = 2.0 + 0.50x → at x = 4.0 ly, ct = 4.0 ly. Q (ct = 2.0 ly) lies below → earlier in S′. Lorentz: γ = 1.155; cΔt′ = γ(0 − 0.50 × 4.0 ly) = −2.3 ly.

questions.q: A student draws the world line of an electron moving at constant velocity as a straight line at 50° to the ct axis. Which evaluation is correct?
options: It cannot be correct: tan 50° ≈ 1.2, so the electron would have to move faster than light.
It cannot be correct: a line at more than 45° would mean that the electron moves back in time.
It is possible: the angle to the x axis is 40°, so its speed is c tan 40° ≈ 0.84c.
It is possible: sin 50° ≈ 0.77, so the electron is moving at a speed of about 0.77c.
optionWhy: tan θ = v/c gives v = 1.19c. No particle with mass can reach c, so its world line must make less than 45° with the ct axis.
A student who links faster-than-light motion with time travel picks this. The line at 50° still rises in ct, so it does not go back in time; it is impossible because it means v > c.
A student who measures the angle from the x axis picks this. θ in tan θ = v/c is measured from the ct axis; at 50°, v = 1.19c, which is impossible.
A student who uses sin θ picks this. The relation is tan θ = v/c, and tan 50° = 1.19 > 1 gives a speed above c.
questions.explain: tan θ = v/c gives v = 1.19c. No particle with mass can reach c, so its world line must make less than 45° with the ct axis.
questions.working: v/c = tan 50° = 1.19 > 1 → impossible for a massive particle. (tan 40° = 0.84; sin 50° = 0.77 are the errors.)

questions.q: In a simplified muon experiment, muons moving at 0.995c (γ = 10.0) are counted at 1000 per hour by a detector on a mountain. An identical detector 2.25 km lower counts about 700 per hour. The muon half-life at rest is 1.5 μs, and the descent takes 7.5 μs in the Earth's frame. Which conclusion do the data support?
options: Time dilation: in the muons' own frame their half-life is dilated to 15 μs, so most survive.
Length contraction: Earth observers measure the 2.25 km drop contracted to about 225 m.
Time dilation: in the Earth frame the half-life is about 15 μs, so about 700 per hour should arrive.
Neither effect: the 1.5 μs rest half-life must be wrong, as half-life is the same in all frames.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a moving particle's time slows in its own frame picks this. In its own frame a muon is at rest with a half-life of 1.5 μs; it survives there because the atmosphere is contracted.

A student who assigns length contraction to the wrong frame picks this. The mountain is at rest in the Earth frame, so Earth observers measure 2.25 km; the contraction to 225 m is measured in the muons' frame.

Earth frame: half-life = γ × 1.5 μs = 15 μs, so the 7.5 μs descent is 0.5 half-lives and 1000 × 2^(−0.5) ≈ 710 per hour survive, as observed. Without time dilation the descent is 5 half-lives and only about 31 per hour would arrive.

A student who assumes time intervals are the same in every frame concludes the rest-frame value must be wrong. The measured half-life at rest is reliable; the data match the relativistic prediction of a dilated half-life.
questions.explain: Earth frame: half-life = γ × 1.5 μs = 15 μs, so the 7.5 μs descent is 0.5 half-lives and 1000 × 2^(−0.5) ≈ 710 per hour survive, as observed. Without time dilation the descent is 5 half-lives and only about 31 per hour would arrive.
questions.working: Earth frame: descent time = 2250 m/(0.995 × 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) = 7.5 μs. Dilated half-life = 10.0 × 1.5 μs = 15 μs → 0.50 half-lives → 1000 × 2^(−0.50) = 7.1 × 10² per hour ≈ observed 700. No dilation: 7.5/1.5 = 5.0 half-lives → 1000 × 2^(−5.0) ≈ 31 per hour. Muon frame: drop contracted to 2250/10.0 = 225 m, crossed in 0.75 μs = 0.50 half-lives → same prediction.
